full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Oral Prescriptions: Receipt, Follow-Up and Emergency Dispensing
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Receipt duties, follow-up documentation, Failover and emergency dispensing
learning_objectives: Carry out the pharmacist's duties at the moment an oral controlled-substance prescription is received.
Choose the follow-up period from the route the prescription travelled, and identify who owes it.
Separate the Schedule VI Failover from an ordinary electronic-prescribing outage.
State which sovereign's follow-up period actually binds an emergency oral Schedule II prescription dispensed in Massachusetts.
Describe what the emergency follow-up must carry on its face and what the pharmacist does with a paper follow-up as against an electronic one.

orientation.text: Massachusetts starts from the position that an oral prescription is not an ordinary format choice. Under 105 CMR 721.020(A) every prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be an electronic prescription unless it is issued under one of the exceptions listed in 105 CMR 721.070, so a lawful oral prescription is always the downstream product of some exception. That framing matters for the pharmacist because the exception that opened the route also decides the follow-up period, the acceptable form of the follow-up, and in one narrow case whether any follow-up is owed at all. The pharmacist's own duties at the moment of the call do not vary with the route: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires the oral prescription to be reduced to writing immediately on a prescription form carrying the prescriber, the patient, the drug and strength, the directions and cautionary statements, the pharmacy's serial number and the refill information, and s. 20(b) requires a reasonable effort to determine that the authorization came from a registered practitioner where that practitioner is not known to the pharmacist.

The follow-up architecture comes from two sources and produces three different periods, and the exam turns on keeping them apart. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) states the default: a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription must cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy within 2 days. The same subsection then diverts a practitioner who has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h) to a WRITTEN prescription within not more than 7 days, or the shorter period federal law requires, postmarked within that period. Separately, 105 CMR 721.070(B) governs a practitioner who issues an oral prescription for a controlled substance in Schedules II through V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) exception: a written or electronic prescription within not more than seven BUSINESS days, or the shorter period federal law requires. In every version the deadline belongs to the practitioner rather than to the pharmacist, the follow-up must say on its face that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the writing it already made. Schedule VI sits outside s. 20(c) entirely.

Two routes look alike from the counter and are not the same. A Failover is defined in the definitions section of 105 CMR 721.000 as a document that ORIGINATES AS A SCHEDULE VI ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION, suffers an unforeseen defect during electronic transmission, and is converted to a computer generated facsimile. Under 105 CMR 721.020(G) such a document is considered an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up, provided it carries everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the signature and is immediately entered or reduced to writing, the pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort where the prescriber is unknown, and the prescription is not for an Additional Drug. The ordinary outage is the different thing: 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) excepts prescriptions issued where electronic prescribing is unavailable because of temporary technological or electrical failure, and a Schedule II through V prescription taken on that basis still owes the 721.070(B) follow-up. The schedule is the discriminator, and it sits in the definition rather than in the three conditions beneath it.

The emergency Schedule II pathway is where both sovereigns reach the same prescription and their texts do not match. Under 105 CMR 721.060(A) an Emergency Situation waives the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, and written and oral prescriptions may then be issued but must comply with every other prescription requirement including 105 CMR 721.070(B). Under 721.060(B) a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization, limited to the quantity adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period. Federal law reaches the same dispensing more narrowly: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) permits a Schedule II drug to be dispensed only on a written prescription signed by the practitioner except as paragraph (d) provides, and paragraph (d) opens on the pharmacist RECEIVING ORAL AUTHORIZATION. The federal exception has no written limb at all, so a Massachusetts fact pattern that turns on a written emergency authorization is resting on state law alone.

Choosing the emergency follow-up period is a two-step trip through the Massachusetts text rather than a contest between two sovereigns. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations as an ePrescribing exception, which is why the emergency prescription never sits in the s. 20(c) two-day default: it is in the proviso by definition. 105 CMR 721.060(A) then routes it to 721.070(B), and 721.060(B)(4) states the same period directly, both as seven business days. But 721.070(B) states its period subject to any SHORTER period required by federal law, and 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription. Seven calendar days expires before seven business days, so the federal period is the one that actually binds, reached through the Massachusetts regulation rather than around it. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) says the same thing from the other side when it requires the follow-up to comply with federal and state law.

The record layer is the part candidates skip. On the emergency call the pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing carrying everything otherwise required except the practitioner's signature. When the follow-up arrives, 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires its face to carry BOTH the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing AND the date of the oral order, and it splits the pharmacist's handling by medium: a paper follow-up is ATTACHED to the oral prescription earlier reduced to writing, while for an electronic follow-up the pharmacist must ANNOTATE the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. If the practitioner never delivers, the pharmacist must notify the nearest DEA office, and the pharmacist's own failure to notify voids the authority that permitted the dispensing in the first place. Any written follow-up must additionally satisfy 105 CMR 721.020(F): the practitioner's signature, and either transmission by facsimile or similar technology or a tamper-resistant form, because a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones on a Thursday afternoon. A patient discharged that morning needs an immediate dose of a Schedule II analgesic, and the prescriber says an electronic prescription cannot be transmitted before the patient needs it. You dispense a three-day supply. Your intern asks when the follow-up prescription is due, and offers two candidate answers: two days, or seven business days.
steps: Identify the route. This is an Emergency Situation, and 105 CMR 721.060(A) waives only the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system while leaving every other prescription requirement in force.

Reject the two-day answer. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) sets its two-day electronic default for a practitioner who has received no electronic-prescribing exception, and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates emergency-situation prescriptions as exactly such an exception.
Follow the Massachusetts routing. 105 CMR 721.060(A) sends the prescription to 105 CMR 721.070(B), and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the same period directly: seven business days.

Read the whole of 721.070(B). Its period is not more than seven business days OR SUCH SHORTER PERIOD THAT IS REQUIRED BY FEDERAL LAW, so the Massachusetts count is a ceiling rather than an entitlement.

Supply the federal period. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription, and seven calendar days expires before seven business days.
Count from the right event. The federal clock runs from the practitioner's authorization of the oral prescription, not from the date you dispensed or the date the patient collected the drug.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither of the intern's answers is the operative deadline. Massachusetts counts seven business days, but its own regulation defers to any shorter federal period, and the shorter federal period is the 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) running from the oral authorization. The error the scenario invites is quoting the Massachusetts seven business days as though it were extra time.

worked_examples.scenario: On day six a follow-up for an emergency oral Schedule II dispensing arrives as an electronic prescription rather than on paper. It bears the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing but nothing else unusual. A technician prints it, staples it to the writing you made on the telephone, and files the pair.
steps: Confirm the timing is satisfied. The follow-up arrived inside the operative federal 7-day period, and 105 CMR 721.070(B) accepts a written OR an electronic prescription, so nothing turns on the medium for the deadline itself.

Check the face against the whole federal requirement. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the face to carry the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing AND the date of the oral order; the phrase alone leaves the requirement half met.

Correct the handling. The attach-and-file step is the federal instruction for a PAPER follow-up. For an electronic prescription the pharmacist must annotate the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.
Note that printing the electronic prescription does not convert it into the paper document the attachment rule addresses, so the annotation on the electronic record is still owed.
worked_examples.resolution: The filing is not compliant. The face notation is incomplete without the date of the oral order, and an electronic follow-up is annotated on its own record rather than discharged by stapling a printout. The error the scenario invites is treating Authorization for Emergency Dispensing as the whole face requirement and treating attachment as the only handling rule.

worked_examples.scenario: Your electronic prescribing connection is down for the afternoon. A prescriber telephones an oral prescription for a Schedule IV benzodiazepine, and separately a Schedule VI prescription arrives as a computer generated facsimile after its electronic transmission failed. A colleague says both are Failovers, so neither needs a follow-up prescription.
steps: Apply the Failover definition before its conditions. A Failover is a document that originates as a SCHEDULE VI electronic prescription, suffers an unforeseen transmission defect, and is converted to a computer generated facsimile.

Classify the Schedule IV order. It was never a Schedule VI electronic prescription, so it cannot be a Failover regardless of the outage; it falls under the separate 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) exception for temporary technological or electrical failure.

Give the Schedule IV order its follow-up. As an oral Schedule II through V prescription issued under a 721.070(A) exception it owes a written or electronic prescription within not more than seven business days under 105 CMR 721.070(B).

Test the Schedule VI facsimile against the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G), including that it is not for an Additional Drug, and verify it before relying on it, since an electronic prescription transmitted by other means is otherwise invalid.
Keep the pharmacist's own duties in place for both: immediate reduction to writing and a reasonable effort to authenticate a prescriber who is not known to you.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague is half right. Only the Schedule VI facsimile can be a Failover, and only if all three conditions hold; the Schedule IV oral prescription still owes a seven-business-day follow-up. The error the scenario invites is reading the three Failover conditions as the whole test and skipping the Schedule VI limit in the definition above them.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Two things must be written on the face of the federal emergency follow-up prescription. Name both.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, and the date of the oral order (21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A paper emergency follow-up is attached. What must the pharmacist do instead when the follow-up is electronic?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Annotate the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts measures the emergency Schedule II follow-up in seven business days. What period actually binds, and why?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The federal 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4), running from the oral authorization, because 105 CMR 721.070(B) states its own period subject to such shorter period as federal law requires and seven calendar days expires first.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 721.060(B) lets a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II substance on the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization. Does the federal emergency exception have the same two limbs?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens only on the pharmacist receiving ORAL authorization, so the written limb is a Massachusetts feature with no federal counterpart.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Give the three Massachusetts oral-prescription follow-up periods and the route each belongs to.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Two days electronic under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) where the practitioner has received no exception; not more than 7 days written where the practitioner has received a s. 23(h) exception; not more than seven business days written or electronic for an oral Schedule II through V prescription issued under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) exception.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why is a Massachusetts emergency oral prescription never governed by the two-day electronic default?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) enumerates prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations as an ePrescribing exception, and the two-day default applies only where the practitioner has received no such exception.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which schedule must a document have started in to be a Failover, and what does a verified Failover excuse?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedule VI, and it excuses the written or electronic follow-up prescription that an oral prescription would otherwise owe.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A written follow-up arrives on a plain prescription pad, signed. What is the format problem?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires a written prescription either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form, and 105 CMR 721.040(A) makes a non-conforming format invalid and not fillable.

quick_review.text: On receiving an oral controlled-substance prescription the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information Massachusetts requires, and must make a reasonable effort to authenticate a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.

The statutory default is an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is available only where the practitioner has RECEIVED an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner, and that follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI.

Where the oral prescription for a Schedule II through V substance was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions, the regulation gives the practitioner not more than seven BUSINESS days and accepts either a written or an electronic prescription.

Most electronic-prescribing exceptions are categorical and are held by nobody: they attach to the prescription's circumstances, such as a veterinarian, a temporary technological failure, an emergency, or Schedule VI. Only a time-limited waiver is applied for and held.

A Failover is a Schedule VI device by definition: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, suffered a transmission defect, and was converted to a computer-generated facsimile. Only such a document counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up.

In a Massachusetts Emergency Situation a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization, limited to the quantity adequate for the emergency period, with the practitioner owing a follow-up within seven business days. The federal exception in 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens on oral authorization alone.

The emergency follow-up must carry Authorization for Emergency Dispensing AND the date of the oral order on its face; the pharmacist attaches a paper follow-up and annotates an electronic one with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.

A Massachusetts emergency oral prescription is issued under an enumerated ePrescribing exception, which is why 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes its follow-up to 105 CMR 721.070(B) rather than to the two-day electronic default.

decision_logic.condition: An oral controlled-substance prescription is received by telephone.
decision_logic.action: Reduce it to writing immediately with the required Massachusetts information, and authenticate the prescriber if that practitioner is not known to you.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber has not received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner.
decision_logic.action: Expect an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is not open to that prescriber.

decision_logic.condition: The oral Schedule II through V prescription was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions.
decision_logic.action: Expect a written or electronic follow-up within not more than seven business days, and treat a shorter federal period as controlling where one applies.

decision_logic.condition: The document began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission, and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile.
decision_logic.action: Only then consider the Failover route, and only if all three of its conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug; otherwise the ordinary follow-up duty stands.

decision_logic.condition: A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission of a Schedule II through V prescription.
decision_logic.action: That is the ordinary outage exception, not a Failover. The prescription may be issued orally or in writing, and the follow-up duty remains.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist dispenses a Schedule II controlled substance on oral authorization in an emergency.
decision_logic.action: Limit the quantity to the emergency period, reduce the prescription to writing at once, and authenticate an unknown prescriber. For the follow-up, count seven business days under 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) and 721.070(B) but treat the shorter federal period as the operative one: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires delivery within 7 days after the practitioner authorized the emergency oral prescription, and 721.070(B) states its own period subject to that shorter federal period. Check the follow-up's face for Authorization for Emergency Dispensing and the date of the oral order, attach a paper follow-up or annotate an electronic one, and notify the nearest DEA office if it never comes.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked whether an emergency Schedule II authorization may arrive in writing rather than by telephone.
decision_logic.action: Separate the sovereigns. 105 CMR 721.060(B) accepts the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization, but 21 CFR 1306.11(d) opens only on oral authorization, so a written emergency authorization has no federal counterpart and the federal Schedule II written-prescription requirement in 1306.11(a) is what such a document must otherwise satisfy.

decision_logic.condition: You must decide whether the two-day electronic default or the seven-business-day route governs an emergency oral prescription.
decision_logic.action: Recognise that the Emergency Situation is itself the ePrescribing exception under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4), so the prescription sits in the proviso rather than the default and 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes it to 105 CMR 721.070(B).

ma_vs_federal.text: For an emergency oral Schedule II prescription Massachusetts measures the practitioner's follow-up in seven BUSINESS days while the federal rule allows seven days from the oral authorization, so the federal period is the shorter one and controls.

Both Massachusetts follow-up provisions carry the qualifier that a shorter federally required period controls, and the federal period they point at is the seven days for an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up.

Massachusetts opens its emergency Schedule II route on the practitioner's WRITTEN OR ORALLY TRANSMITTED authorization under 105 CMR 721.060(B), but federal law has no written route at all: 21 CFR 1306.11(d) is an ORAL authorization exception to the signed-written-prescription rule in 1306.11(a). The written limb is therefore a Massachusetts formulation with no federal counterpart, and repeating it without that qualifier overstates what an emergency permits on federally reachable facts.

Federal law splits the pharmacist's handling of the follow-up by medium and Massachusetts does not: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires a paper follow-up to be attached and an electronic one to be annotated with the original authorization and the date of the oral order, while 105 CMR 721.060(B)(5) states only the attachment step.

exceptions.text: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, and the statutory follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI either.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an exception or waiver.

The three Failover conditions sit downstream of the definition. Meeting all three does nothing for a prescription that was never a Schedule VI electronic prescription converted to a computer-generated facsimile.
An emergency waives only the electronic-prescribing requirement; every other prescription requirement continues to apply to the written or oral prescription the emergency permits.

Dispensing beyond the emergency period is not covered by the oral authorization; the federal exception limits the quantity to the amount adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period and requires a signed paper or electronic prescription for anything further.
A central fill pharmacy is not authorized under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(5) to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization received from a retail pharmacist or a practitioner.
Unlike the time-limited waiver route, the Emergency Situation exception is not applied for and held by the practitioner; it attaches to the situation itself.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner electronic follow-up after an oral controlled-substance prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the statutory default where the practitioner has received no electronic-prescribing exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner written follow-up where the practitioner has received a commissioner's exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: A mailed written prescription must be postmarked within the period.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under an enumerated exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: Seven business days is a longer span than seven calendar days; either a written or an electronic prescription discharges it.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up after emergency oral Schedule II dispensing
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Seven business days under 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4); 7 days under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The federal 7 days runs from the practitioner's authorization of the emergency oral prescription and is the shorter period, so it is the operative deadline; 105 CMR 721.070(B) states its own period subject to it.

timing_deadlines.event: Pharmacist's failure to notify the DEA when no emergency follow-up arrives
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No separate period; the consequence attaches to the omission
timing_deadlines.consequence: The authority conferred by 21 CFR 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription is voided.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing on a prescription form with the prescriber, patient, drug, directions, serial number and refill information Massachusetts requires.

The follow-up prescription must indicate on its face that it is issued to document an oral prescription, and on receipt the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it had reduced to writing; the pharmacist's record is incomplete until the two are joined.

A written follow-up must itself satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules: the practitioner's signature, and either transmission by facsimile or similar technology or a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements.

An emergency follow-up prescription must bear on its face BOTH the words Authorization for Emergency Dispensing AND the date of the oral order, as 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires and as 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) imports when it directs that the follow-up comply with federal and state law. A mailed paper follow-up must be postmarked within the period.

How the pharmacist files the emergency follow-up depends on its medium: a paper follow-up is ATTACHED on receipt to the oral emergency prescription earlier reduced to writing, while for an electronic follow-up the pharmacist must ANNOTATE the record of the electronic prescription with the original authorization and the date of the oral order.

The emergency oral prescription is reduced to writing carrying everything otherwise required except the practitioner's actual signature, and it may be entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system instead of being written out.

role_duties.duty: Reduce the oral prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber, join the follow-up document to it on arrival, and notify the DEA where an emergency follow-up never comes.
Deliver the follow-up prescription within the period that applies to the route the prescription travelled, in the form that route accepts.
Notify the nearest DEA office when an emergency follow-up is not delivered, understanding that omitting the notification voids the authority relied on to dispense without a written prescription.

Determine that the Emergency Situation elements are met before authorizing an oral Schedule II prescription, and deliver the follow-up bearing the required face notations within the shorter of the applicable periods.

common_traps.text: Calling any transmission outage a Failover waives a follow-up the law still requires; a Failover is Schedule VI by definition, and an outage affecting a Schedule II through V prescription is a different exception entirely.
Reading the three Failover conditions as the whole test misses the definitional limit sitting above them.
Treating every electronic-prescribing exception as something the prescriber holds misreads the list; most attach to the circumstances of the prescription and nobody applies for them.
Quoting seven days and seven business days as though they were the same period gets a follow-up delivered on day nine wrong in one direction or the other.
Looking only for a paper follow-up misses that the regulation accepts a written or an electronic prescription.

Applying the Massachusetts seven business days to an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up ignores the shorter federal 7 days in 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4), which 105 CMR 721.070(B) itself defers to; the Massachusetts count is a ceiling rather than extra time.
Accepting a follow-up on a form no permitted format supports leaves the file resting on an invalid prescription, which may not be filled at all.
Reading Authorization for Emergency Dispensing as the whole face requirement drops the date of the oral order, which 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires alongside it.
Carrying the Massachusetts written-or-orally-transmitted emergency authorization into a federal answer invents a written route that 21 CFR 1306.11(d) does not contain.
Answering two days for an emergency oral prescription applies the default to a prescription that is always issued under an enumerated ePrescribing exception.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws c. 94C

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: On receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance, the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C §20 and make a reasonable effort to authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber; the subsection requiring later electronic or written documentation expressly does not apply to Schedule VI.
exceptions: The follow-up prescription requirement in §20(c) does not apply to Schedule VI, but immediate reduction to writing and validity duties still apply.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.

full_prose_under_review.title: Prescriptions from Out-of-State Practitioners
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Three pathways, their windows, and the duties each places on the pharmacist
learning_objectives: Identify which of the three out-of-state pathways the facts fall into before reaching for any number.
Apply the correct presentation window: 30 days for schedules III through VI, 5 days for either schedule II route.
Apply the authenticity duty to every pathway and the telephone-verification duty to the pathways that carry it.
Separate the window on the prescription from the five-day limit on an initial partial dispensing.
Carry out the post-fill reporting duty the schedule II pathways impose.

orientation.text: Massachusetts does not have one out-of-state rule; it has three, and they sit in adjacent subsections of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18. Subsection (c) covers schedules III through VI issued by an authorized practitioner licensed and registered where they reside or practise. Subsection (d) covers a NONNARCOTIC schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner. Subsection (d1/2) covers a NARCOTIC schedule II prescription, and narrows the issuing states to Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth. The first question on any out-of-state fact pattern is which of the three you are in, because the window and the duties both change.

The windows are the easy half. A schedule III through VI prescription may be filled here only if it was issued within the preceding 30 days. Either schedule II route runs on five days instead. Neither window is a federal clock: the federal six-month schedule III and IV period does not license a prescription Massachusetts no longer treats as fillable, because the presentation window is the earlier gate and it closes first.

The duties are where candidates go wrong. Every one of the three subsections places a duty on the FILLING PHARMACIST to determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. On top of that, subsection (c) adds telephone or other verification only where the substance is in schedules III to V, while subsections (d) and (d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for their schedule II routes. The practical shape is counter-intuitive: verification is NOT a schedule III to V speciality, and schedule VI is the single pathway that carries the authenticity duty without it. On every pathway a pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which verification cannot be obtained, and is protected from liability for refusing where good faith efforts were documented.

Two duties survive the fill itself. If the prescription is a schedule II filled under (d) or (d1/2), the pharmacist must deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the FILLING, with the patient's name and address removed. And if such a prescription is partially dispensed, a separate five-day limit governs the initial partial dispensing while the remainder still closes 30 days after the issue date. Two different five-day rules therefore live in this area, one about when the prescription may be presented and one about when an initial partial dispensing must be completed.

worked_examples.scenario: A New Hampshire physician's written prescription for amphetamine salts, a nonnarcotic Schedule II substance, is presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy three days after it was issued. The prescriber is registered in New Hampshire and under federal law. Your technician says verification is only needed for Schedules III through V. What do you do?
steps: Identify the pathway. A nonnarcotic Schedule II from an out-of-state practitioner is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d), not s. 18(c) and not the narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2).
Check the window. s. 18(d) authorizes filling only where the prescription was issued within the preceding five days; three days is inside it.

Apply the duty the pathway states. s. 18(d) requires the filling pharmacist both to determine authenticity and validity in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment and to verify the prescription by telephone or other means. The technician is wrong: verification is not a Schedule III through V speciality.
If verification cannot be obtained, do not fill. Document the good faith efforts; the statute protects a pharmacist who refuses on that basis.
After filling, start the post-fill clock: a copy goes to the Department within 30 days of the filling, without the patient's name and address.
worked_examples.resolution: Verify before filling. Skipping verification here would fill a Schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill, and the Department copy is still owed 30 days after the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Connecticut nurse practitioner's prescription for a Schedule VI antihypertensive is presented 20 days after issue. Your colleague wants to telephone the prescriber's office to verify before filling, and is frustrated that nobody is answering after hours. Must the fill wait for that call?
steps: Identify the pathway. Schedule VI from an out-of-state practitioner falls under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches schedules III to VI inclusive.
Check the window. s. 18(c) authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 days; 20 days is inside it.

Read the duty precisely. s. 18(c) imposes the authenticity-and-validity determination on every prescription it reaches, but conditions telephone or other verification on the substance being in schedules III to V. Schedule VI is outside that condition.

So the pharmacist still has to be satisfied, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid -- but the separate telephone-verification duty is not triggered.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The fill does not wait on a verification call that this pathway does not require. Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the telephone-verification duty, and this is the distinction the wording of s. 18(c) turns on.

worked_examples.scenario: A Rhode Island physician's oxycodone prescription, a Schedule II narcotic, is presented four days after issue. The patient asks for only part of the quantity today. Which five-day rule are you applying, and what closes when?
steps: Identify the pathway. A narcotic Schedule II from a contiguous state is s. 18(d1/2), and Rhode Island is contiguous with the commonwealth.
The first five-day rule is the presentation window: s. 18(d1/2) authorizes filling only where the prescription was issued within the preceding five days. Four days is inside it.
Verify the prescription by telephone or other means, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.

The second five-day rule is different: the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2) must be filled not more than five days after the prescription issue date. That also lands on day five, but it is measuring the dispensing rather than the presentation.
The remaining portion runs on its own clock: not later than 30 days after the issue date, and only at the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity.
worked_examples.resolution: Both five-day rules are satisfied today, and they are not the same rule. Note the partial dispensing and quantity in the patient record, keep any remainder at this pharmacy, complete it within 30 days of the issue date, and send the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of the filling.

full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as a Massachusetts prescription-drug classification rather than a federal controlled schedule.

orientation.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI is the residual schedule: it holds prescription drugs that Massachusetts has not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V. Schedule VI has no federal counterpart, so the ordinary prescription drug that carries no federal schedule is, in Massachusetts, a Schedule VI controlled substance. Two consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Because Schedule VI is not a federal schedule, Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled, and federal controlled-substance mechanics do not automatically travel with the label. Because Schedule VI is nonetheless a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule, a Massachusetts rule that speaks to controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless that rule carves Schedule VI out. Reading the label as a synonym for unregulated is the single most productive source of wrong answers in this area.

Everything that governs a Schedule VI prescription is Massachusetts law, but it does not come from one regulator. M.G.L. c. 94C is the statute above both. The Department of Public Health writes 105 CMR 700.000 and 105 CMR 721.000, and from there come the classification itself, the prescription-format scheme, the electronic-prescribing exceptions and the prescription monitoring program. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy writes 247 CMR, and from there come the dispensing and refilling rules, the within-date counting convention, the customer identifier and the transfer framework. That division is why a Schedule VI question can present two different one-year rules that sit in two different chapters and answer two different questions: 247 CMR 9.04(12) says how long the prescription stays valid, and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) says how long it stays transferable. Neither restates the other, and a candidate who has collapsed them into one rule will misread whichever question is actually being asked.

On format, Massachusetts starts from a default that every prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be electronic, and then lists the prescriptions excepted from it. Schedule VI is one of the enumerated exceptions, at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9), which is why a Schedule VI prescription may lawfully arrive written or oral. The exception is narrow in exactly the way candidates tend to forget: it lifts the electronic-format mandate and nothing else. A written Schedule VI prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled. An oral Schedule VI prescription must still be reduced to writing immediately with the information the statute requires. The one duty Schedule VI genuinely escapes is the practitioner's later follow-up prescription, because M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) says by its own terms that it does not apply to Schedule VI. The Failover device points the same way: it is defined as a document that originates as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, so no other schedule can produce one.

A Schedule VI prescription can be stopped by more than one clock, and the exam rewards knowing which clock the facts have started. The general one is the validity limit: a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year. A second one attaches to the prescriber rather than the drug. An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription for filling in Massachusetts, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and it is that paragraph, not the one-year rule, that makes the out-of-state prescription fillable here in the first place. Both clocks are counted the same way, because in determining whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. When the applicable clock has run, the only thing left is the narrow professional-judgment continuation, and that is conditioned on the pharmacist being unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner rather than being available for the asking.

Transfer is the other place where the Schedule VI label changes the analysis, and it does so in the pharmacy's direction as well as the patient's. Under 247 CMR 9.14 a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and it may act as the patient's agent to facilitate that transfer. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription, so neither a standing refusal to transfer nor a transfer charge is a matter the pharmacy gets to decide for itself. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III through V prescriptions, carrying up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, subject to the separate one-year transfer bar. Schedule VI is also the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform the transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

Finally, the Schedule VI label is not a promise that no monitoring or identification duty will ever attach. The Commissioner may determine that a drug is an additional drug for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012 because it carries a bona fide potential for abuse, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion, or a known contribution to overdose. On making that determination the Commissioner notifies all dispensers that they must begin reporting the dispensing of that drug. Once a Schedule VI drug is an additional drug, dispensing it requires a customer identifier from the ultimate user or their agent, the data go to the Department by the end of the next business day covering everything dispensed since the previous transmission, and the Failover route closes, because a Failover does not qualify where the prescription is for an additional drug. The label describes the starting point, not the whole of the drug's regulatory position.

No. A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued ten months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. Pharmacy A says it does not transfer prescriptions as a matter of store policy, and that if it did it would charge the patient a transfer fee first. Pharmacy B has a certified pharmacy technician available and the pharmacist on duty approves the technician's participation.
steps: Classify the drug before anything else. It is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V, so it is Schedule VI, and the federal transfer mechanics do not reach it because Schedule VI is not a federal schedule.

Check the age of the prescription against the transfer bar rather than the validity clock. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued; ten months is inside that limit.

Test Pharmacy A's policy against 247 CMR 9.14(1). A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, so a standing refusal to transfer cannot stand against the request.
Test the fee against 247 CMR 9.14(3), which provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. There is no discretion to price the transfer.

Settle what moves. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V, and may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, so all three remaining refills may travel.

Settle who may act. A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and that authority is confined to Schedule VI; do not generalise it to any other schedule.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer proceeds promptly, without a fee, carrying the three remaining refills, and the certified technician may carry it out with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is treating a no-transfer policy and a transfer charge as pharmacy discretion, when 247 CMR 9.14(1) and 9.14(3) remove both; a second error is reaching for a six-month cutoff in place of the one-year transfer limit.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule VI prescription written forty-five days ago by a practitioner licensed and registered in New Hampshire, whose address on the prescription is a New Hampshire office. The patient points out that Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions are good for a year, so the prescription must still be fillable.
steps: Confirm the patient is right about the clock they have named. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) the prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and forty-five days is well inside that.

Then ask the question the patient has not asked: what makes an out-of-state practitioner's prescription fillable in Massachusetts at all. That authorization is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches prescriptions in Schedules III to VI inclusive.

Read the limit that paragraph attaches to its own grant. It is valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, so it is a second date gate rather than a restatement of the first.
Count the days the way the Board directs, taking the day after the prescription was written as day one. Forty-five days still falls outside the thirty-day window however the count is started.

Do not look for a verification step that will rescue it. The express duty to verify the prescription by telephone or other means runs to Schedules III through V; for a Schedule VI prescription the pharmacist's duty is the general one to determine that the prescription is authentic and valid, and neither duty extends the thirty-day window.
worked_examples.resolution: The prescription may not be filled on the out-of-state authorization, because the paragraph that authorizes filling it here reaches only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days. The error the scenario invites is answering from the one-year Schedule VI validity clock alone and never asking where the prescriber wrote from.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient arrives on a Saturday evening out of a maintenance medication. The Schedule VI prescription on file was issued fourteen months ago and shows refills that were never used. A colleague says the prescription has plainly expired, so the fourteen-day continuation is simply what you dispense in that situation.
steps: Establish that the prescription itself is spent. It was valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year, so unused refills on a fourteen-month-old prescription do not survive the expiry.

Read the continuation as the conditional allowance it is. It opens where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills AND the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner; the inability condition governs the expiry branch exactly as it governs the no-refills-remaining branch.

Attempt the authorization first. Try the prescriber, or whoever is covering, and record the attempt. Only once authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner does the professional-judgment allowance become available at all.

If it does open, respect the ceiling. The pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity not to exceed fourteen days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. It is a bridge, not a refill, and it does not renew the expired prescription.

Check the setting before applying any of this. 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), so the validity clock and the continuation attached to it do not reach that facility type.
worked_examples.resolution: Attempt the prescriber before dispensing anything; the fourteen-day continuation becomes available only after that attempt fails to produce timely authorization. The error the colleague makes is reading the expiry branch as self-executing, which drops the inability-to-obtain-authorization condition the regulation attaches to both branches.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts Schedule VI carries two separate one-year rules. State each one and what it measures.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(12): a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c): a pharmacy may not transfer a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date the prescription was issued. One measures fillability, the other transferability.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy tells a patient it does not transfer prescriptions, and that in any event it charges for a transfer. Which two provisions dispose of that?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and 247 CMR 9.14(3) provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Besides the one-year validity clock, what second date gate can stop a Schedule VI prescription, and where does it come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c): an authorized out-of-state practitioner's prescription in Schedules III to VI inclusive may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which oral-prescription duty does Schedule VI escape, and which does it keep?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It escapes the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up prescription, which states that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI. It keeps the duty to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately with the information the statute requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception sits at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does it not excuse?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It lifts the electronic-format mandate only. The statutory prescription elements still apply, a written prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What turns an ordinary Schedule VI drug into one carrying monitoring and identification duties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Commissioner's determination that it is an additional drug carrying a bona fide potential for abuse. On that determination dispensers are notified that they must begin reporting it, a customer identifier is required at dispensing, and the data go to the Department by the end of the next business day covering everything dispensed since the previous transmission.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile. What is it, and what does it not owe?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Failover. It is considered an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G) hold and the prescription is not for an additional drug.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written; the issue date itself is not counted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Beyond the statutory element list, name three things 105 CMR 721.020(D) requires on the prescription itself.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity of dosage units; a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled; and, for a schedule II opioid, the notation that the patient may request less than the full quantity. 721.020(E) adds the supervising professional's name for certain nurse prescribers.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program and requires a customer identifier at dispensing.

A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and may act as the patient's agent to facilitate the transfer; a standing policy of refusing transfers cannot displace that duty.
A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized; the federal one-time transfer limit does not reach it, because Schedule VI is not a federal schedule.

A prescription written by an authorized out-of-state practitioner is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive and authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days; that is a second date gate on a Schedule VI prescription, distinct from the one-year validity clock.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Act on the request rather than declining it: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, 9.14(2) lets the pharmacy act as the patient's agent to facilitate it, and 9.14(3) forbids charging a fee for the transfer. Then apply the Schedule VI mechanics under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription transfers in the same manner as a Schedule III through V prescription and may carry up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars the transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry it out with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription has expired, being presented more than one year after its issue date, or has no refills remaining, and in either case the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it. The inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization conditions both branches equally, so attempt the prescriber first in the expired case exactly as in the no-refills-remaining case. Only once that attempt has failed may the pharmacist, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier and treat the dispensing as reportable, using the documented hardship route only on its own terms.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI prescription was written by a practitioner licensed and registered outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Apply the out-of-state date gate before the validity clock: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling such a prescription only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days, counting the day after it was written as day one. Determine that the prescription is authentic and valid; note that the express telephone-or-other-means verification requirement runs to Schedules III through V rather than to Schedule VI.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts classification and does not itself make a drug federally controlled.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

The Massachusetts route for an out-of-state practitioner's prescription is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive; because Schedule VI has no federal counterpart, that thirty-day window is a purely Massachusetts limit and has no federal analogue to be read against it.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Schedule VI validity clock, the day-counting convention and the customer-identifier duty all fall away for that facility type.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception.

The Failover is a Schedule VI device: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, provided its three conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling in Massachusetts a Schedule III through VI prescription issued by an authorized out-of-state practitioner
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within that window, so an older out-of-state Schedule VI prescription is barred even though the one-year validity period has not run.

timing_deadlines.event: Transmission of prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By the end of the next business day
timing_deadlines.consequence: Each transmission carries every controlled substance dispensed since the previous one.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.
A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug; the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed and signed name and address.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) requires a practitioner who dispenses a controlled substance by issuing a written or electronic prescription to state on it the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date of delivery of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Read that as the list the statute itself imposes, not as a closed inventory of everything a Massachusetts prescription must carry: the Massachusetts prescription-format regulations reach the same prescription and impose their own requirements alongside the statute.

The format regulation states the prescription's required content beyond the statutory element list: 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires the QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit; (D)(6) requires a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled; and (D)(4) leaves the patient name and address blank not only on a veterinary prescription but also on one for naloxone or another Department-approved opioid antagonist and on one issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12).

A prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also carry the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Act on a patient's or agent's transfer request in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and transfer without charging a fee.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

Treating a refusal to transfer, or a charge for transferring, as a matter of pharmacy discretion overlooks the affirmative timely-transfer duty in 247 CMR 9.14(1) and the fee prohibition in 247 CMR 9.14(3).

Treating the one-year validity clock as the only date gate on a Schedule VI prescription misses the separate thirty-day limit M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) places on an out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription.

Reciting the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) elements as the complete set of content and exception rules for a Massachusetts prescription treats a statutory list as exhaustive, when the prescription-format regulations govern the same prescription in their own right.

Naming the veterinary prescription as the only case where the patient's name and address may be left blank misses the naloxone and opioid-antagonist limb and the two ePrescribing-exception limbs in 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

Commissioner exceptions permitting written and oral prescriptions
Follow-up documentation for an oral prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, although the immediate reduction to writing and the remaining validity duties still apply.
A shorter federal period controls where federal law requires one, such as the 7-day emergency oral Schedule II follow-up under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

authority.name: Prescription formats for written prescriptions
Invalid prescriptions
Written prescription form requirement

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).

authority.name: Definition of Failover
Failover treated as an oral prescription
Invalid prescriptions, Failover exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.010 defines a FAILOVER as a document that ORIGINATES AS A SCHEDULE VI ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION, experiences an unforeseen defect during electronic transmission as outlined in Department guidance, and IS CONVERTED TO A COMPUTER GENERATED FACSIMILE. Only such a document qualifies. Under 105 CMR 721.020(G) a Failover SHALL BE CONSIDERED AN ORAL PRESCRIPTION and SHALL NOT REQUIRE a written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided all three conditions hold: it contains everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or otherwise reduced to writing by the dispensing pharmacist; if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the dispensing pharmacist, that pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the Failover was issued by a prescribing practitioner; and the prescription is NOT FOR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG as defined in 105 CMR 700.001. Under 105 CMR 721.040(C) an electronic prescription transmitted by other means is invalid except in the event of a Failover verified under 721.020(G). A Schedule II through V oral prescription taken during a transmission outage is NOT a Failover; it falls under the separate 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) exception and still owes the 721.070(B) follow-up.
exceptions: A Failover is Schedule VI by definition; no Schedule II through V prescription can be one.
The three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)(1)-(3) are conjunctive, and they apply only after the definitional test is met.
A Failover for an Additional Drug does not qualify, so the follow-up duty continues to apply to it.

authority.name: Prescription Monitoring Program transmission

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) the information 105 CMR 700.012 requires shall be transmitted to the Department or its agent, in accordance with any procedures the Commissioner establishes, BY THE END OF THE NEXT BUSINESS DAY, and shall include data for ALL CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES DISPENSED SINCE THE PREVIOUS TRANSMISSION or report, by encrypted electronic device or electronic transmission method in a format the Commissioner approves. Under 700.012(A)(6) the Commissioner may waive that method for a pharmacy unable to submit electronically.
exceptions: The Commissioner may waive the electronic transmission method for a pharmacy unable to submit by electronic means.

authority.name: Out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription filled in Massachusetts within 30 days of issue; Schedule III through V prescriptions require pharmacist verification.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Prescription formats, required content

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.020(C) requires the practitioner's NAME AND ADDRESS to be clearly indicated on the Prescription, and a hospital or clinic Prescription to carry the name and address of the hospital or clinic. 105 CMR 721.020(D) requires the Prescription to contain: (1) the REGISTRATION NUMBER of the practitioner; (2) the DATE OF ISSUANCE; (3) the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance prescribed, AND THE QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS; (4) the NAME AND ADDRESS OF THE PATIENT, except in a veterinary Prescription, a Prescription for naloxone or another opioid antagonist approved by the Department, or a Prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12), in which case the name and address may be left blank, and where the person taking delivery of a naloxone or other approved opioid antagonist Prescription MAY, but is not required to, be used in place of the patient's name; (5) DIRECTIONS FOR USE, including any required cautionary statements; (6) a STATEMENT INDICATING THE NUMBER OF TIMES TO BE REFILLED; and (7) for an OPIOID substance in schedule II, a NOTATION THAT THE PATIENT MAY FILL THE PRESCRIPTION, UPON REQUEST, IN AN AMOUNT LESS THAN the recommended full quantity indicated. Under 105 CMR 721.020(E) a Prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also contain the NAME OF THE SUPERVISING qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice under 244 CMR.
exceptions: The patient name and address may be left blank on a veterinary prescription, a naloxone or other Department-approved opioid antagonist prescription, or a prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12).
The supervising-professional name is not required where the issuing nurse is authorized for independent practice under 244 CMR.
